title: Conversation zipper merge procedure (brain dump)
content:
Top-level intent:
This is a personal scratchpad for a "zipper" merge strategy to reconcile concurrent conversation fragments from clients/edge proxies with the central session state. The mental model: align two sequences (base, incoming) as if zipping them together using token/utterance anchors and metadata (author, timestamp, intent tag). The goal: produce a deterministic, explainable merged timeline that preserves user intent, minimizes hallucination from merged assistant deltas, and makes rollbacks/simple reverts possible.

Context / why: We have cases where mobile clients prefetch, offline-edit prompts, or tool-execution-driven deltas come back and attempt to patch a live session. Simple last-write-wins loses continuity; naive append duplicates things or overwrites assistant responses. We need a lightweight, low-latency merge that can run in the ingestion path (or as an asynchronous reconciliation pass) and produce minimal semantic distortion.

Design goals (non-exhaustive):
- Deterministic: same inputs -> same merge result.
- Minimal intervention: prefer merging at utterance boundaries when possible.
- Attribution-aware: maintain who said what and when (client-generated vs server-generated).
- Explainable: return a merge journal describing applied operations for audit and debugging.
- Reversible: maintain a compact undo manifest for fallback.
- Cheap: avoid heavy semantic understanding in the hot path; heuristics and lightweight token-based alignment only.

Key concepts / terminology:
- fragment: a contiguous series of messages/turns sent from a client or agent to be applied to a session.
- base: authoritative session timeline prior to applying the incoming fragment.
- anchor: small stable token sequence or message id used to align fragments (e.g., last user message id, system instruction checksum, or short token suffix).
- zipper merge: iterative merge walking two sequences and resolving conflicts using heuristics.
- patch op: {retain, insert, replace, tombstone} as operations in the returned journal.

Heuristic rules (first cut):
1) Try anchor-first alignment: if fragment includes an explicit anchor id that exists in base, align fragment start there and treat subsequent deltas as insertions after anchor.
2) Fuzzy token-suffix match: if no id, look for a short suffix (8-64 token hash) of the fragment first user turn in base; if found, align.
3) Utterance-level mapping: split both base tail and fragment into utterances (speaker boundary). Prefer to merge by inserting missing utterances rather than replacing, unless content overlap >= 85% token similarity AND the fragment author is assistant with "correction" metadata.
4) Assistant delta guardrails: never replace an assistant utterance unless the incoming assistant fragment has explicit replace_reason and monotonic timestamp newer than assistant's prior turn, and the client signature is from an administrative/operator path. This prevents accidental assistant rewrite by a client replay.
5) Conflict resolution priority: user edits > client-local-tool-run > assistant-generated (lowest). Within same source, prefer higher timestamp (deterministic tie-breaker: lexical client_id if timestamps equal).
6) Duplicate suppression: identical messages by exact text match are suppressed (idempotent). Near-duplicates (>= 98% token overlap) are collapsed with an annotation linking both origins.

Example merge scenarios (sketch):
A) Offline user typed a follow-up while disconnected; server already produced an assistant response from a teammate proxy. The fragment contains anchor = user-msg-339. We align and insert user follow-up after user-msg-339; assistant response remains and becomes older in timeline (assistant may be stale). If the follow-up should have changed assistant content, that is left to downstream application-level re-generation (we do NOT auto-delete assistant outputs).

B) Two clients both attempted to correct system instruction in the same session. They both send patches modifying system scope. We treat system scope as high-priority; both patches become explicit "system edits" and we return a merge journal with two system-version entries; latest wins for an active system checksum, but both edits are available in history and for a canary rollback.

API sketch (hot-path merge endpoint)
POST /sessions/{session_id}/merge\payload: {
  fragment_id: string,
  client_id: string,
  anchor_id?: string,
  messages: [ {id?, role: user|assistant|system|tool, text, ts, meta? } ],
  signature?: string,
  intent_hint?: string
}
response: {
  merged: true|false,
  ops: [ {op: retain|insert|replace|tombstone, target_id?, msg_id?, reason, applied_by } ],
  resulting_tail_checksum: string,
  undo_manifest_id?: string
}

Note: The shapes above are intentionally lightweight (all strings). We'll need to map to internal protobufs later. Keep ops small — only include events touching the tail N turns (configurable).

Zipper algorithm (pseudocode, rough):
- Let A = last k utterances in base (k configurable; default 64 utterances or 2048 tokens).
- Let B = incoming fragment utterances.
- i=0; j=0; ops = []
- while i < len(A) and j < len(B):
    if match(A[i], B[j]) -> ops.push(retain A[i]); i++; j++;
    else if A[i] is close-match to B[j] (>= 85%) and source(B[j]) higher-priority -> ops.push(replace A[i] with B[j]); i++; j++;
    else if B[j] appears to be insertion (next B[j+1] matches A[i]) -> ops.push(insert B[j]); j++;
    else if A[i] appears stale (next A[i+1] matches B[j]) -> ops.push(tombstone A[i]); i++;
    else -> ops.push(insert B[j]); j++;
- append remaining B[j:] as insert ops
- any trailing A[i:] are retained by default
- return compact ops, journal, resulting checksum

Match heuristics: exact id -> match; fallback token overlap or edit-distance threshold. Use locality-sensitive hashing for token suffix match in practice.

Audit / observability needs:
- Merge journal persisted per-session with small retention (7-30 days) and linked to trace id.
- Telemetry counters: merges/second, conflicts/merge, replace_ops/merge, latency_p50/p90.
- Sampling: on conflict > threshold, capture full pre/post and store in long-term snapshot bucket (for evaluation).

Undo / fallback plan:
- Generate undo_manifest: list of inverse ops (reverse-ordered) sufficient to revert the applied ops. Keep it small by only recording operations touching last k turns. Persist undo_manifest id in response.

Open questions / TODOs (my rough priority list):
- How big should k be? Tradeoff: larger k gives better alignment but slows hot path. Start with k=32 utterances / 1024 tokens.
- Should we do a semantic-based merge (embedding similarity) for assistant content? Probably not in hot path, but a background reconciliation job could run evaluations and surface required re-generations.
- Anchoring UX: need client SDK helpers to emit compact anchor checksums to improve alignment probability. Define stable anchor strategy (e.g., final 256-token rolling hash of last user message).
- How to expose merge journal to end-users (CS/debugging) vs customers (privacy). Mask tool outputs as needed.
- Operational: rate-limit merge attempts per session to avoid churn loops (client stuck repeatedly sending new fragments).
- Security: validate signature for fragments that propose assistant replacements.

Notes to self:
- Add unit tests for: exact-id alignment, fuzzy-suffix alignment, replace guardrail, revert manifest generation.
- Mock some conflicting traces and run the zipper in a test harness (Ethan / Ravi, want you to pair on this).
- Create a small benchmark for latency: median target 2ms extra on merge hot path. Anything >10ms needs push to background.

Rough next steps (implementation plan):
1) Implement core zipper library as pure Go module with pluggable matchers.
2) Wire endpoint into proxy ingestion path behind a feature flag. Start with async path (enqueue, short timeout).
3) Add telemetry + journaling. Provide debug endpoint to fetch last merge journal for a session.
4) Iterate heuristics after running on a sample of production traffic.

Slack notes / references:
- earlier convo: slack://thread/runtime-merge-experiments/xyz
- related ticket: JIRA-SSW-927 (session patch reconciliation)
- possible follow-up GH work: GH-PR-4821 (zipper library initial commit)

Random brainstorming snippets (unstructured):
- Could we use a compact Crdt-like tombstone id scheme for assistant deltas to make replacement reversible? maybe overkill.
- For UX, surface a subtle flag in SDK: "merge_mode: optimistic|conservative" so client can choose risk appetite.
- Consider a "merge_preview" API for editors that want to show user the merged timeline before confirming (useful for collaborative docs).

End of brain dump.
